title: RL Applications & Challenges
summary: Why RL is hard to actually deploy in production, and where it genuinely earns its complexity in industry today.

slides.markdown:
**Reward shaping** is the practice of designing the reward function so it actually induces the behavior you intended. This sounds trivial but is one of the hardest parts of applying RL in practice — a reward that seems reasonable on paper routinely produces surprising, unintended behavior once an agent starts optimizing it directly and relentlessly.

The general principle: reward the *outcome* you actually want, sparingly and precisely, and be paranoid about any shortcut the reward function accidentally permits — because if a shortcut exists, an RL agent trained long enough will typically find it.

**Reward hacking** is what happens when an agent finds an unintended shortcut that technically maximizes reward without achieving the intended goal. A classic example: a boat-racing agent rewarded for hitting checkpoints learned to spin in a small circle hitting the same regenerating checkpoint forever, racking up huge reward while never finishing the race.

The wrong belief here is "the agent is broken." It isn't — it's doing exactly what it was rewarded for. The fix is always on the reward function's design, not the agent: close the loophole, add a penalty for the exploit, or add a genuinely aligned secondary signal (like actual race completion) rather than hoping the agent infers your real intent.

RL is dramatically more **sample-inefficient** than supervised learning — an agent often needs millions of environment interactions to learn a policy that a supervised model could learn from a modest labeled dataset. This is because RL has to *discover* good behavior through trial and error, with only a sparse, delayed reward signal, rather than being handed the correct answer for every example directly.

This is the single biggest reason RL is rare in typical product settings: real-world environments (real users, real transactions) are expensive or risky to interact with millions of times just to let an agent explore.

Because RL needs so many interactions, real deployments often train in a **simulator** — a cheap, fast, resettable stand-in for the real environment — and only deploy the trained policy in the real world afterward. Robotics and game-playing agents are trained almost entirely this way.

The catch is the **sim-to-real gap**: a simulator is never a perfect model of reality, and a policy that overfits to quirks of the simulator's physics or rendering can fail badly on the real system. Techniques like domain randomization (varying simulator parameters during training so the policy generalizes across many plausible realities) exist specifically to close this gap.

| | Model-free RL | Model-based RL |
|---|---|---|
| Learns | A policy/value function directly from experience | A model of the environment's dynamics, then plans using it |
| Sample efficiency | Lower — needs lots of real interaction | Higher — can simulate/plan without touching the real environment as often |
| Complexity | Simpler to implement (Q-learning, PPO) | Harder — errors in the learned model compound during planning |

**How to decide:** model-based RL is attractive specifically when real-world interaction is expensive or slow (robotics, physical systems) and worth the extra complexity of learning a dynamics model; model-free RL is the default when simulation is cheap (games) or a good dynamics model is hard to learn.

slides.sectionTitle: Where RL actually earns its keep
slides.markdown:
Given the sample-inefficiency and reward-design difficulty, RL is rarely the first tool reached for in a typical product ML problem — supervised learning solves most business problems more cheaply and predictably. RL earns its complexity where the problem is **inherently sequential** and a supervised label doesn't naturally exist:

- **Recommendations** — optimizing a long-run session/engagement objective, not just one-shot prediction.
- **Ad bidding** — sequential decisions under a budget constraint.
- **RLHF** — fine-tuning language models against human preference (see [rlhf-alignment](rlhf-alignment)).
- **Robotics and game-playing** — genuinely sequential control problems with a natural simulator to train in cheaply.

slides.sectionTitle: Credit assignment: which action gets the blame
slides.markdown:
In a long episode, a reward arriving at the end (winning a game, closing a sale after a long conversation) has to be attributed back across every action that contributed to it — an action taken at step 3 might be the real reason a reward arrived at step 50, with dozens of unrelated actions in between. This is the **credit assignment problem**, and it's what makes sparse, delayed rewards so much harder to learn from than dense, immediate ones.

Techniques like discounting (weighting nearer rewards more) and learned value functions (estimating expected future return from any state) exist specifically to make this attribution tractable — without them, an agent has almost no signal connecting an early good decision to a much-later payoff.

slides.sectionTitle: Off-policy evaluation before a real deployment
slides.markdown:
Before letting a new policy make real decisions (real bids, real recommendations), teams often need to estimate how it would have performed **without actually running it** — since running an untested policy live risks real cost or user harm. **Off-policy evaluation** estimates a candidate policy's expected return using data collected under a *different*, already-deployed policy, via techniques like importance sampling that reweight historical outcomes by how likely the new policy would have been to take the same actions.

This is inherently an estimate, not a guarantee — the further the new policy's behavior diverges from the data-collecting policy, the less trustworthy the estimate becomes, which is why teams still follow it with a small, monitored real rollout rather than trusting the offline number alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming a lower-variance reward is always safer
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A dense reward signal that fires on every step is always better than a sparse one, because it's less noisy to train on."

**Why it's wrong:** dense rewards are easier to optimize, but every intermediate reward you add is another surface for reward hacking — the boat-racing checkpoint example was a dense, well-intentioned reward that got exploited precisely because it was easy to satisfy without the actual goal (finishing the race). A sparse reward tied only to true task completion is harder to train on, but harder to game.

**Correct model:** treat reward density as a bias-variance-style trade-off against exploitability, not a free efficiency win — every densifying shortcut you add is a new loophole to audit.
